A hole found later is a finding against this file, and it is named in this list rather than left to a reader to discover

not_carried.sqlite: the runner installs it from Debian's packages into /usr/bin, and the editor copies only /opt and /usr/local out of the runner

runs_as.set_to: the uid:gid that owns the mounted sources on the host
runs_as.why: a container that runs as root writes root-owned files into the mounted sources, and the reader can then never edit their own repository
runs_as.how: the base image's fixuid repairs the passwd record and the ownership of the home directory for whatever uid the consumer ran it as; the editor's entrypoint runs it before it seeds anything, so a uid other than 1000 starts

workspace.why: the workspace ROOT is not in the image, so docker would create it root-owned and no build could write .gradle/, .kotlin/ or build/ into it; a named volume there is root-owned for the same reason. A tmpfs is world-writable, holds only those scratch directories, and is discarded with the container. The source binds sit inside it

filesystem.why: the image must be able to write outside the mounts. The entrypoint's fixuid repairs the passwd record before it seeds anything, so /etc is written at every start; and the warmed practice caches live under /opt, where Gradle and Maven write on every build. A read-only root filesystem, or a mount that makes one of these read-only, breaks the editor at start or breaks every graded run in it
filesystem.what_is_discarded_with_the_container: everything outside editor.mounts: the workspace root is a tmpfs and the rest of the writes are the container's own layer

mounts.purpose: the corpus's sources, and nothing else: not the repository, not $HOME
code-server's user data: the settings the entrypoint seeds once, and the reader's own edits
the Gradle user home the entrypoint seeds from the prime when it is empty; omit it when gradle is not declared
the Maven local repository the entrypoint seeds from the prime when it is empty; omit it when maven is not declared

ports.why: an unencrypted IDE with a shell AND NO PASSWORD (see command_notes.auth). 0.0.0.0 offers it to every machine that can reach this host; loopback is the WHOLE of this service's access control, so widening this field is not a deployment preference but a decision to put an unauthenticated shell on the network

environment.name: GRADLE_USER_HOME
environment.note: explicit rather than derived from $HOME, so the seeded cache and the tool agree

command_notes.auth: --auth=none is EXPLICIT AND LOAD-BEARING, and the explicitness IS the decision: code-server's default when --auth is absent is password, so an omitted flag is a different setting, not this one. Register ruling 2026-09-22, replacing the earlier ruling that the editor always required a password. THE BOUNDARY IS THE PORT, NOT THE PASSWORD: ports[0].host_bind is 127.0.0.1, so the only clients that can reach this IDE are processes on this host -- the same trust boundary the study site already publishes on unauthenticated, and any process inside it could read PASSWORD out of the container's own environment anyway. The password stopped no reader it was meant to stop and cost a login form inside every practice iframe. THE CONDITION IS THEREFORE THE BIND: if host_bind is ever widened past loopback, or publish_on_all_interfaces is ever set true, this flag goes back to --auth=password IN THE SAME EDIT. tests/test_consuming.py asserts the two together for exactly that reason.
command_notes.bind_addr: 0.0.0.0 INSIDE the container only, which is the container's own interface; the loopback restriction is the ports entry's host_bind
command_notes.replaces_cmd: a compose command: replaces the image's CMD outright, and the image re-declares ENTRYPOINT and CMD so nothing the base bakes is appended to it
command_notes.extensions_dir: the extensions are installed into the image, not onto a volume, so an image upgrade carries them
command_notes.workspace_trust: --disable-workspace-trust is LOAD-BEARING and is not a preference: without it the lockdown was once installed and never ran. A corpus's sources arrive as a bind mount, which the workbench has never been told to trust, and a workbench in Restricted Mode disables every extension that does not declare support for one -- silently, with no error and no log line. Measured on code-server 4.137.0: studyforge.practice-focus was installed, listed and never activated, and the Java debug and test extensions were disabled in the same sessions. The image's own CMD carries it too, so a consumer who does not set command: gets it; a consumer who does set command: must keep this argument.

prime.why: a reader's own build in the editor's terminal starts from a cache warmed with the corpus's own dependencies, so the first build needs no download; the same prime directory the runner is built with, and a corpus that declares none is unaffected

healthcheck.why_this_interpreter: code-server's own node, which every declared set carries; a set without python has no python3 and a set without node has no node on PATH
healthcheck.ordering: a consumer whose own service creates one of the bind sources gates this one on it with depends_on: <service>: condition: service_healthy, so the editor starts after the directory exists

editor.why_no_docker_socket: spec 8.3: the Docker socket is never mounted into a serving process, not behind a flag and not only locally. This is an IDE with a shell published on a port

extensions.the_command_surface_is_confined: a reader inside a practice frame cannot open the command palette, Go to File, Search for Text, Quick Chat, Go to Symbol, Start Debugging, Run Task, the settings editor or the settings JSON. The mechanism is an ALLOW-LIST of what a practice needs (lockdown/allowed.js), from which every other default keybinding's removal is DERIVED against the workbench's own default keybinding document -- a deny-list would be wrong the next time the workbench gains a command and nothing would say so. The tab guard in the extension is the other half, because removing a keybinding does not unregister a command: any editor tab that is not the file that window's URL opened is closed, whatever opened it. What a practice needs still works: editing the one file, saving it, and the study page's own Run and Submit.
extensions.why_it_is_integrity_and_not_tidiness: files.readonlyExclude is what makes a Submit mean anything -- the test that judges the reader is not theirs to edit -- and it is an OBJECT setting, which VS Code MERGES across scopes. Measured on code-server 4.137.0 in a real session: a workspace value of {\"Main.java\": true} became {\"MainTest.java\": true, \"Main.java\": true} after one ConfigurationTarget.Global write, and the user settings file on disk carried it. A reader who can reach the settings editor can therefore make their own test writable, so confining the command surface is an integrity clause and not a tidiness one.
extensions.keybindings_are_the_lockdowns_file_not_t: The image seeds <user data dir>/User/keybindings.json on EVERY start, unlike settings.json which is written only when absent. Two reasons, both measured: the workbench reads the user keybindings file when a SESSION STARTS and ignores a write made while one is open, so it has to be in place before any session exists; and a user-data volume from an earlier image would otherwise keep a keybinding the allow-list no longer permits. A consumer who wants a different set changes the allow-list and rebuilds -- an edit to the file inside a volume does not survive a restart.
extensions.must_run_not_merely_be_installed: installed is not running: the image is tagged only after a real workbench session in it showed the extension host activating studyforge.practice-focus and the extension announcing that it ran (docker/editor/activation.py), AND a headless browser pressed Ctrl+Shift+P, Ctrl+P, Ctrl+comma, F5 and the rest at that same session and nothing opened, while the editor's own find widget still opened and what was typed still reached the file on disk (docker/editor/confinement.py). A consumer that replaces command: and drops --disable-workspace-trust takes that guarantee away again, and nothing in the image can put it back.

runtimes.why_no_default: a corpus declares what its practices need, and the image carries exactly the union that set places under /opt; an empty set builds the base and nothing else

runs_as.why_powershell_differs: run_value is a POSIX shell substitution: PowerShell on Windows has no id and a Windows user has no uid. Docker Desktop hands the files a container writes into a Windows bind to the Windows user whatever uid wrote them, so an ordinary user that is not root is the whole requirement there
runs_as.why_compose_value: the same value the editor block's runs_as renders, which compose interpolates on every host and every shell: HOST_UID and HOST_GID are set by the consumer where the host has a uid, and the default is an ordinary user where it has none
runs_as.set_to: the uid:gid that owns the mounted source root on the host
runs_as.why: this image declares no USER, so without the flag a graded run writes root-owned build output into the reader's own sources and the reader can then never edit their own repository
runs_as.how: there is no fixuid here and none is needed: nothing under HOME is seeded, HOME is a world-writable path outside the mount, and the only directory a run writes is the bind

workspace.opened_by: the image's WORKDIR, and the -w of every docker exec
workspace.why: the corpus's source root and nothing else. A graded run reads and writes the reader's own sources in place, so unlike the editor there is no tmpfs to discard and no copy to keep in step

mounts.purpose: the corpus's source root, and nothing else: not the repository, not $HOME

network.why: a graded run resolves what it needs from the caches the prime warmed into the image. Nothing it does reaches off the machine, so a practice cannot pass because the reader happened to be online

runner.why_no_ports: nothing in this image listens: it idles on its CMD and every command arrives through docker exec. A published port would be a surface with no service behind it

init.why: the container idles on `sleep infinity` as pid 1, which reaps nothing; without an init a stopped run leaves zombies behind and the stop itself is slow

environment.name: HOME
environment.note: chosen once in docker/minimal/plan.py's RUNNER_HOME and read by the Dockerfile, so no tool writes its caches into the mounted sources

command_notes.keeps_cmd: the run line passes no command: the image's own CMD idles it, and replacing that is how a consumer gets a container that exits before the first exec arrives
command_notes.path: PATH is set for docker exec and again in /etc/profile.d, because a login shell rebuilds PATH and would otherwise lose /opt

run.documented_in: README.md, under 'Running it for a corpus'
run.why_rendered: the README's line and this block are the same sentence twice. A test asserts the documented one is what this block renders, so prose that drifts is a red test rather than a stale instruction a consumer follows

prime.why: a reader's graded run happens in this image under --network none, so a corpus's practice dependencies are already inside it; a corpus that declares none is unaffected

runner.why_no_healthcheck: nothing here answers a request. A consumer that must wait asks docker whether the container is running and execs a command that exits zero, which is what the framework's runner does before it uses one
runner.why_no_docker_socket: spec 8.3: the Docker socket is never mounted into a serving process, not behind a flag and not only locally. A socket here would hand a graded run - which is a reader's unreviewed code - the host's daemon
runner.why_restart_no: the reader starts this container for a session of study and removes it after; a restart policy would bring a stranger's sources back up on every boot
